issue_context.title: Add rich type for reading X509 Authority Information Access
comments:
Tagging subscribers to this area: @dotnet/area-system-security, @vcsjones See info in [area-owners.md](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/area-owners.md) if you want to be subscribed.
Issue Details
One of the standard X.509 extension types defined by RFC 3280 (and successive RFCs) is the "Authority Information Access" extension. The use case is largely to inform chain building engines where any OCSP endpoints might be, and where one might find a copy of the issuing CA's certificate. With a lot of handwaving, this extension can be thought of an order series of 3-tuples: * What kind of purpose is this for? (OCSP endpoint, where to download a CA cert, some future/private purpose) * What type of data is present? (the most useful type here is URI, other options include an LDAP X.500 identifier, or an email address, or an IP address... most of which don't make sense in context) * What is the value? (legal encodings are determined by the data type) For a typical .NET caller, the most important information is the URI-typed values for OCSP or the issuing CA. Rather than muddy the type with all of the complexities of modelling everything, the type is limited mostly to these common cases and anything more complicated can be accomplished with `AsnReader`. ```C# namespace System.Security.Cryptography.X509Certificates { public sealed partial class X509AuthorityInformationAccessExtension : X509Extension { public X509AuthorityInformationAccessExtension() { } public X509AuthorityInformationAccessExtension(ReadOnlySpan encoded, bool critical = false) { } public override void CopyFrom(AsnEncodedData asnEncodedData) { } public IEnumerable EnumerateCAIssuersUris() { throw null; } public IEnumerable EnumerateOcspUris() { throw null; } public IEnumerable EnumerateUris(string accessMethodOid) { throw null; } } } ```
Author: bartonjs
Assignees: -
Labels: `area-System.Security`
Milestone: 7.0.0

My original inclination was to say that this type couldn't be used to craft the extension because of ordering and accessMethod.  But two options present themselves that I'm interested in discussing:

* `.ctor(IEnumerable<string> ocspEndpointUris, IEnumerable<string> caIssuersUris, bool critical=false)`
  * Writes all OCSP endpoints before all CA issuers... because that's the order their OIDs sort
* `.ctor(IEnumerable<(string AccessMethodOid, string UriValue), bool critical=false)`
  * Requires a much less pleasant invocation, but lets ordering be explicitly controlled, and supports future/private access methods (but not the other "7" GeneralName data types)

I originally thought the first option was kind of dirty, because it's so "opinionated".  But it's probably the 99.99% use case and the 0.01% can use AsnWriter.

> that this type couldn't be used to craft the extension because of ordering and accessMethod

I see the utility in such API. There have been some mentions in [previous issues](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/59191) to the effect of "I am trying to build a CA in .NET". Someone that is trying to build such functionality will eventually want to be able to add these extensions to a `CertificateRequest`.

> But two options present themselves that I'm interested in discussing

"Why not both" is a possibility.

A third possibility is to consider a `X509AuthorityInformationAccessBuilder` such as we have with SANs and now X500DNs. There is an appeal to (to me) separate the writer and reader concepts, and the builders can be more ergonomic where ordering is explicit (by way of whatever order `AddXYZ` is called). It also gives more flexibility in the future to improve, I would think, by just introducing new `AddBanana` methods.

Alternatively, if `GeneralName` ever does become a rich type, then the extension could probably just gain another constructor to support it.

I don't feel very strongly about a `Builder` for it. It certainly feels a bit niche to me.

> proposal

Should there be:

```csharp
public X509AuthorityInformationAccessExtension(byte[] encoded, bool critical = false)
public X509AuthorityInformationAccessExtension(AsnEncodedData encodedAuthorityInformationAccess, bool critical);
```

The `byte[]` is just a matter of "we tend to offer byte overloads where we have span APIs". The second I don't see a big need for, but, every other `X509Extension` derived type has it, so it's a question that comes from the perspective of consistency.

> `public X509AuthorityInformationAccessExtension(AsnEncodedData encodedAuthorityInformationAccess, bool critical);`

All the extensions do with the AsnEncodedData is throw if they're null (usually NullReferenceException), and then pass data.RawValue down to the base ctor (ignoring data.Oid).  Basically, I cut out the middleman.

> `public X509AuthorityInformationAccessExtension(byte[] encoded, bool critical = false)`

That's fair.

> A third possibility is to consider a `X509AuthorityInformationAccessBuilder` such as we have with SANs and now X500DNs.

Yeah, that was my starting position.  Then, when explaining in the issue prose why the type couldn't be used to craft the extension (and that the builder would come later) I felt like maybe we could get several 9s of coverage from either of those two options.

> "Why not both" is a possibility.

If we think that `.ctor(IEnumerable<string> ocspEndpointUris, IEnumerable<string> caIssuersUris, bool critical=false)` will cover enough use cases then I'd rather leave out the value-tuple-accepting version.

The builder might allow for some complicated expression of interleaving, other GeneralName value kinds, and future access method items... but using AsnWriter directly for it isn't really all that hard: https://github.com/bartonjs/runtime/commit/ef1e54866e56737d7ec4e60c76e2f0c89ecf9d66#diff-18b898e9da53598005170588ef8a5297095a5f10f14f66367006c1ad7f464f4aR504-R533

I think I'm growing in confidence that `.ctor(IEnumerable<string> ocspEndpointUris, IEnumerable<string> caIssuersUris, bool critical=false)` is a good starting point, and then we can let feedback guide us to something more complicated... if it's ever warranted.
Renamed the `encoded` ctor parameters to `rawData` to match the name on X509Extension, and added the (IEnumerable,IEnumerable,bool) ctor for building the extensions.

>  I just don't want "Use AsnWriter" to be a fallback that gets too comfortable.

I generally agree.  But I'm OK with "Use AsnWriter" to be "you're doing something rare/weird"; and as we learn something is less rare/weird we can add easier-to-use public API.

> Or, more specifically, should ocspEndpoints be ocspUris?

Looks like it.

I thought that RFC 3280 or 5280 called it "OCSP endpoint", but "endpoint" appears in neither of those documents.  So "ocspUris" seems correct and consistent.

review_comments:
Maybe overkill, but since these methods are `IEnumerable<...>` do you think there is value in a test that creates the enumerator multiple times and they are distinct enumerators?

```
_ = aia.EnumerateOcspUris().ToArray(); // Create an enumerator and consume it
Assert.Equal(expected, aia.EnumerateOcspUris()); // Different, functional enumerator.
```
What happens if the extension ends up with no `AccessDescription`s? The RFC syntax is `SEQUENCE SIZE (1..MAX) OF AccessDescription`. So you need at least one. Should this error, or let it slide?

I had originally thought about making it throw...

As far as I can tell, neither Windows nor OpenSSL validate the sequence count on decode or encode; and all the rest of the extension types have... some sort.. of default behavior.  For this one "be empty" seemed to make sense for that default state.

That's when I added the "empty" test, to show that it was intentional that it worked.

@bartonjs just as one more point of data, Apple rejects that cert: `security verify-cert -d 2022-05-21-00:18:00 -c deleteme.pem -r deleteme.pem -p basic` produces: Certificate errors 0: test Unable to parse a standard extension (corrupt or invalid format detected) [UnparseableExtension] It seems that in Big Sur, Apple tightened their cert parsing logic, and this feels particularly similar to https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/40944.

I think if I were to suggest anything is that the constructor that builds from the `IEnumerable<string>` parameters should make sure at least one entry is added. Parsing from `rawData` would not throw.
OK, if macOS is going to reject them then I agree we should identify that you tried to build one, but gave no data, and fail early.
Does it matter whether this uses rawData or RawData?  It looks like the latter is just a clone of the former.
For well behaved apps it doesn't matter. For multi-threaded writes, using the property is more consistent with the delayed reads from, e.g., loading the data in via CopyFrom(AsnEncodedData).

How about a test for testing decoding failures?

1. No sequence.
2. Sequence of something else.
3. Trailing data.
